meta.name: Eric Champ
meta.title: Eric Champ — Full-stack & AI Engineer
meta.description: Eric Champ builds production-shaped systems end to end: RAG pipelines, ML scoring, real-time Go and Rust services, cross-border commerce, dataviz and native iOS.

hero.lede: I join teams to get real products out the door: the ML core, the services around it and the interface on top. I measure my work by what the team delivers, so everything I write is tested, readable and ready for the next engineer to build on.

pipeline.label: How every change reaches production · demo loop

work.title: Work a team can build on
work.lede: Every project is a real repository: the algorithm, the schema, the tests and the UI, because a team can only build on what actually works. Each entry states the outcome it was built for. Web projects are live.

projects.title: Docstream RAG
projects.blurb: Retrieval-augmented answers over 40k support documents. Hybrid BM25 + pgvector search, reranking, and citations that link back to the exact paragraph.
projects.outcome: Support team answers tickets from one screen instead of searching three wikis.

caseStudy.context: A 12-person support team at a B2B SaaS company, 40k pages of product docs across three wikis.
caseStudy.problem: Agents spent the first minutes of every ticket searching. Answers were inconsistent and escalations to engineering were climbing.
caseStudy.approach: Hybrid search (BM25 + pgvector) with a reranker, citations to the exact paragraph, and a feedback loop that flags stale documents. Shipped behind a feature flag, measured against a control group for four weeks.
caseStudy.result: Median handling time fell 38%. Escalations to engineering dropped by a third. The team owns the index refresh job and the eval suite without me.

projects.title: Riskgrade
projects.blurb: Gradient-boosted credit risk scoring with calibrated probabilities, SHAP explanations per decision and a reviewer UI for overrides.
projects.outcome: Risk reviewers see why a score was given, so overrides are rare and auditable.

projects.title: Ledgerline
projects.blurb: Order-matching engine in Go with a price-time priority book, deterministic replay from a Kafka log and sub-millisecond p99 under load tests.
projects.outcome: Replayable log means the team can reproduce any incident instead of guessing.

projects.title: Fareframe
projects.blurb: Airline revenue management: EMSR-b seat allocation across fare classes with demand forecasting and a what-if dashboard for analysts.
projects.outcome: Analysts test pricing scenarios themselves, without waiting on engineering.

metric.label: time to run a pricing scenario

projects.title: Crossmarket
projects.blurb: Cross-border checkout with live FX, landed-cost duties per HS code, multi-currency settlement and a Stripe-backed payment flow.
projects.outcome: Customers see the full landed price up front, cutting refund requests after delivery.

metric.label: refund requests in the first quarter

projects.title: Pulsewire
projects.blurb: Rust WebSocket telemetry fan-out on Axum and Tokio. Backpressure-aware, 50k concurrent clients on one node, Protocol Buffers on the wire.
projects.outcome: One node replaced a four-node cluster, with the ops runbook handed to the platform team.

projects.title: Gitgraph
projects.blurb: A CLI and web view that renders any repository's history as a readable release story: conventional commits, branches and annotated tags.
projects.outcome: New engineers read the release history in minutes instead of asking around.

projects.title: Cadence
projects.blurb: Native iOS habit tracker in SwiftUI with on-device streak modelling, widgets and CloudKit sync. No account required.
projects.outcome: Shipped to the App Store with a test suite the next maintainer can rely on.

projects.title: Tidewatch
projects.blurb: Interactive dataviz of coastal tide gauges: 30 years of hourly readings rendered with three.js and a custom time-scrubber.
projects.outcome: Researchers explore three decades of data in the browser, no download required.

about.title: The team’s result is the only score that counts.
paragraphs: I’m a full-stack and AI engineer who likes hard problems and clean systems. Over the past decade I’ve worked across the whole stack, from the algorithm at the core up through relational schemas, tested services, HTTP APIs and refined, modern interfaces.

What I optimise for is simple: the team ships, and keeps shipping after I’ve moved on. That means code the next engineer can read and extend, a git history that explains itself, and the boring, reliable choice whenever the clever one would cost the team later.
The range, from RAG pipelines and risk scoring to Go and Rust services, cross-border commerce and native iOS, exists so I can take whichever layer is blocking the team this week.
